description:
Hi, I’m Alexei, and I’m taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge with my brother, Ivan Guchin. I enjoy building software and designing tools that make complex information easier to understand. Ivan is a production engineer who brings experience in process improvement and practical problem-solving.

We’re competing as a two-person team. We’re excited to combine our software and engineering skills to explore NASA’s open data and build a working prototype that addresses a real-world problem.
summary: GeoTwin is a web app that searches the entire land surface of Earth for the places that most closely resemble the candidate sites for a permanent Moon base (the Artemis regions at the lunar south pole) and key Mars exploration sites. We measured the same terrain features (slope, roughness, local relief, and flat and steep fractions) across more than 130,000 windows of 30 km on Earth and compared them with 153 lunar and 43 Martian reference sites. The data comes from NASA LOLA, HRSC/MOLA, HiRISE, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover and ERA5 climate data. The search refines from 30 km down to 10 km and then to 5 or 2 km, and each candidate gets a score that combines terrain, surface and climate. For every site, GeoTwin explains where the analogy holds and where it breaks, one dimension at a time. Users can explore the results on 3D globes of the Moon, Earth and Mars and compare terrains side by side in 3D at the same scale. The method rediscovers the analogs science already uses: 8 of 11 known sites, such as Atacama and Haughton Crater, rank in the top 10%. It also points to new candidates. This matters because astronauts, rovers and equipment must be tested on Earth first, and picking the right test site saves time, money and risk.
details:
GeoTwin: find the Moon and Mars on Earth, and know where they’re not.

Before a rover drives on the Moon or Mars, it rehearses here on Earth. Mars still keeps surprising us. InSight’s heat probe was built to dig 3 m and stopped at about 40 cm because the soil clumped instead of gripping it, on a mission that cost the U.S. $813.8 M. In Gale crater, sharp rocks tore holes in Curiosity’s wheels faster than expected. In Meridiani, Opportunity was stuck in a sand dune for more than five weeks. NASA picks analog sites for their physical similarity to the destination, but we found no global, quantitative catalog that answers two questions: which place on Earth is most like this landing site, and how is it different?

GeoTwin answers both. It doesn’t prevent failures. It helps teams choose where to test.

What it does
GeoTwin measures all of Earth’s land, 130,535 windows of 30 km, the same way it measures the lunar south pole (all 16 Artemis landing regions) and Mars exploration sites. It then gives every site its three closest Earth twins and says, measure by measure, where the match holds and where it breaks.

How it works

  1. Reference relief: NASA LRO LOLA (40 m) for the lunar south pole, NASA MOLA + ESA HRSC (200 m) and NASA HiRISE terrain models for Mars.
  2. Global scan: Copernicus DEM. Each window gets six terrain measures: typical slope, steep slope (p90), flat and steep fractions, relief and roughness.
  3. Comparing three worlds fairly: each measure becomes its percentile within Earth. The Moon is steeper than almost all of Earth, so it gets compared with Earth’s steepest ground instead of an average that fits nowhere.
  4. Coarse to fine: 30 km, then 10 km (156,898 windows), then 5 km (Moon) or 2 km (Mars). Both worlds always use the same window and the same pixel size.
  5. Surface and climate: ESA WorldCover (10 m) supplies bare rock, ice and vegetation. A full year of ERA5 climate via Meteomatics supplies cold, dryness and the daily temperature swing.
  6. Score = 0.5·terrain + 0.25·surface + 0.25·climate. We tested it against 42 different weightings to check that the top results don’t depend on our choice of weights.

What we found

  • High Andes (29.5°S, 69.5°W) ↔ Shackleton crater, Moon: typical slope 14.6° on Earth vs 14.0° at Shackleton, on 98% bare rock. It differs in having about half the relief, plus air, water and Earth’s gravity. A brief search found no studies that use it as a lunar analog.
  • Qaidam Basin, China ↔ Jezero crater, Perseverance’s landing site: the method picked it without being told. Qaidam is already a published Mars analog, which is evidence the method works.
  • Eastern Sahara ↔ Meridiani Planum, Opportunity’s plain: slope 0.85° vs 0.93°, relief 94 m vs 91 m. It differs in heat and in the metre-scale ripples our windows can’t see.

Does it work? Before looking at any results, we fixed a list of analogs science already uses, including Atacama, Haughton crater, Death Valley, the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Mauna Kea and MDRS. Eight of the 11 we could test rank in Earth’s top 10% for both the Moon and Mars, with medians at the 97.8th and 97.5th percentiles. The ones that rank low have a reason: Río Tinto and Pilbara are chemistry and biology analogs, which terrain data can’t see.

The app

  • 3D globes of the Moon, Earth and Mars at the same size, with every twin marked.
  • Find analogs: pick a lunar or Martian site and compare it with its Earth twin in 3D, at the same scale with a shared camera, colored by relief or slope.
  • Mars route planner: draw or import a rover traverse (GeoJSON, GPX or KML) and get Earth routes with matching distance, climbs and slopes for a field rehearsal.
  • A 2D map with featured stories, rankings, a “new sites only” list, the validation results and 11 NASA analog pairs.
  • English and Spanish, a guided tutorial, and two clicks from an Artemis region to its Earth twin.

Impact

  • Mission teams can choose rehearsal sites for each Artemis landing region and Mars site with numbers they can compare.
  • Universities and student rover teams can find terrain near them that matches a real Mars site and plan routes on it.
  • Teachers and the public can explore the Moon, Earth and Mars side by side and see why the Atacama “is Mars” and where that comparison fails.

Why it’s creative

  • It goes from a handful of hand-picked sites to every land window on Earth.
  • Percentiles let three different worlds be compared fairly.
  • “Where the analogy breaks” is part of every result, not a footnote.
  • The route planner moves a Martian traverse onto Earth.

What we took into account

  • Honesty about limits: gravity (0.17 g on the Moon, 0.38 g on Mars), vacuum, thin CO₂ air and radiation can’t be reproduced on Earth. Polar lighting isn’t modelled yet. Artemis coordinates are approximate.
  • Fair resolution: a comparison never uses a pixel finer than the coarser dataset can support.
  • Variety: results must be at least 150 km apart, and each site’s three twins at least 300 km apart, so one desert can’t fill the ranking.
  • Checked data: Meteomatics’ default model gave 1,181 mm/yr of rain in the hyper-arid Puna, so we switched to ERA5.
  • Low cost: open data only. The app runs in the browser, re-running the ranking needs zero climate queries, and it works offline with packaged imagery.

Tools

  • Pipeline: Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, pystac-client, Microsoft Planetary Computer, Pillow), and the Meteomatics API for climate.
  • Web app: TypeScript, Vite, three.js and Leaflet, with end-to-end tests in Playwright, deployed on GitHub Pages.
  • Data: NASA LRO LOLA, NASA MRO HiRISE, NASA MOLA, ESA HRSC, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover and ERA5.
  • Hardware: a laptop.
  • We built it with AI coding assistance (Claude Code and ChatGPT), and we checked every number against the project’s own data.

The Moon and Mars are far away. Their closest twins on Earth don’t have to be a guess.
